newsitem.title: JAPAN: Tokyo stocks likely to seek bottom.
newsitem.headline: Tokyo stocks likely to seek bottom.

text.p: Tokyo's key Nikkei index is expected to seek the bottom of the market this week after posting its biggest one-day drop since April 1995 on Friday, brokers and analysts said.
The Nikkei average held above the major support line of 20,000, but they said it would sink further before it starts to bounce back.
On Friday, the Nikkei 225 closed at 20,276.70, down 667.20 points, or 3.19 percent, from the day before and 743.66 points from its close Nov. 29.
"The 20,000 level will be a psychological support line, but it is very vulnerable," said Chisato Takahashi, fund manager at Credit Suisse Investment Advisory Co.
Participants were stunned by Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's comments on the U.S. markets, which fuelled worries over the recent euphoria on Wall Street and invited sales.
Greenspan's comments were made just before the Tokyo market opened Friday.

Greenspan said in a lecture to a dinner meeting on Thursday that the Federal Reserve must be wary when "irrational exuberance" infects stock and other asset markets because that could end up doing damage to the economy.
"The comment sparked fears over New York stock movements ... and forced people to close their positions ahead of the weekend," Takahashi said.
Investors and dealers had accumulated long positions in the recent rally of well-known companies, which led to Friday's sell-off, brokers said.
Jesper Koll, chief economist at J.P. Morgan in Tokyo, said yen markets were "almost certainly overreacting."
He also said in a commentary: "I think any dip below 20,500 is a buy as large-cap companies will pull off formidable earnings surprises in the coming six to 12 months."

Tim Hayashida, strategist at Merrill Lynch Japan Inc., said the stock index had already reached a point that requires a downward correction and that Friday's sales were exaggerated by Greenspan's comments.
"We have to see very carefully if the New York market will be hurt by the Greenspan comment," Credit Suisse Investment's Takahashi said.
